extracted.intended_audience: statesmen, political leaders, educated readers seeking practical moral and political guidance (readers of sermons/essays on statesmanship and scripture)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for statesmen on using the Bible and historical examples as a practical manual for political judgment and action; guidance on reading history, applying principles, and understanding causes of revolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare present with past to derive moral advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of thoughtfully assimilating the events of our own age to those of the time before us is the means for deriving resignation from general discontent and for building hope from political gloom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read contemporary events against historic precedents so that the present may be judged by general principles drawn from the past; this habit is a moral duty for those with books, leisure and education. Use the collation of present with past to generate steady hope and practical remedies rather than chasing novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read history for general principles, not mere facts
rubrics_metrics.description: If we read history for the facts instead of reading it for the sake of the general principles, which are to the facts as the root and sap of a tree to its leaves, we will be misled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating history like novels or collections of anecdotes; seek the enduring principles that explain events. Beware of answers that explain revolutions by anecdotes or singular causes rather than systemic principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Scripture as a practical manual for political wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: The inspired writings render miracles superfluous where similar circumstances exist, and the principles revealed and examples recorded in Scripture supply guidance for statesmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply scriptural principles and recorded examples to current political circumstances; the Bible offers both particular facts and universal meaning that can guide statesmanship when properly interpreted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not expect wonders; apply revealed truths instead
rubrics_metrics.description: In the infancy of the world, signs and wonders were required to break down superstition, but with each miracle a truth was revealed to act as its substitute; to neglect to apply truths in expectation of wonders is to tempt God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on established principles rather than waiting for miraculous signs. Treat miracles as historical means to establish truths, not as present-day substitutes for judgment or action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret biblical/historical events both particularly and universally
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Scriptures both facts and persons must of necessity have a twofold significance, a temporary and a perpetual, a particular and a universal application; they must be at once portraits and ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using Scripture or sacred history as guidance, look for both the specific circumstance and its wider, symbolic meaning applicable to current affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer symbols over empty allegory in political instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: An allegory is a translation of abstract notions into picture-language that is itself an abstraction; a symbol is characterised by a translucence of the special in the individual, or of the general in the especial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use living symbols (which partake of the reality they represent) to communicate principles to large audiences rather than abstract allegories that leave the masses unmoved or confused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that abstract notions fuel popular action in tumultuous times
rubrics_metrics.description: In periods of popular tumult and innovation the more abstract a notion is, the more readily has it been found to combine with the feelings of a people and with their immediate impulses to action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or shaping political movements, account for how abstract principles (sovereignty, rights, pure reason) can become powerful mobilising forces in moments of upheaval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate habitual interest in history and political thought to be a statesman
rubrics_metrics.description: Without an habitual interest in these subjects a man may be a dexterous intriguer, but never can be a statesman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statesmen should study historical writers and political philosophy (Thucydides, Tacitus, Bacon, Harrington, etc.) and maintain steady intellectual engagement rather than relying on intrigue or opportunism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to speculative/metaphysical systems as causal factors
rubrics_metrics.description: All the epoch-forming revolutions of the Christian world have coincided with the rise and fall of metaphysical systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss abstract or metaphysical thought as irrelevant; ideological and philosophical shifts often precede and shape major political transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the social and moral root causes of revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The causes of revolutions (e.g., the French Revolution) include the rising importance of commercial/manufacturing classes, incompatibility with feudal privileges, spirit of sensuality and ostentation, presumptuous irreligious philosophy, and overrating of mechanical/technical power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze revolutions by tracing socio-economic shifts, moral and cultural decadence, philosophical trends, and institutional oppressions; avoid simplistic or anecdotal explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge that institutions and orders are products of struggle
rubrics_metrics.description: The happy organization of a well-governed society came into being with blood, tempests, and hardship; it was planted with blood and rocked in tempests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not take stable institutions for granted; recognize their historical fragility and the sacrifices that formed them when making policy or advising governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles must flow from and be felt as universal truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Their particular rules and prescripts flow directly and visibly from universal principles; they are understood in exact proportion as they are believed and felt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws and political prescriptions that visibly derive from widely accepted universal principles will have more authority and be more effective; cultivate belief and feeling for these principles among the populace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/political guidance should root in faith (conviction) as well as reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulator is never separated from the main spring. We (that is, the human race) live by faith. Whatever we do or know different from the brute creation has its origin in a determination of the reason to have faith and trust in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and guidance that rely purely on instrumental reason without grounding in moral conviction are fragile; cultivate the deeper convictions that make motives operative in conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prideful complacency about familiarity with sacred texts
rubrics_metrics.description: The main hindrance to the use of the Scriptures as your manual lies in the notion that you are already acquainted with its contents; something new must be presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach canonical texts and classic histories with humility and a readiness to discover new applications; do not dismiss them as exhausted by prior familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensory and illustrative means judiciously to clear barriers to truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The senses were miraculously appealed to to overthrow usurpations exercised through the senses; the natural Sun calls up the breeze to chase away vapours and converts the air into the minister of purification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ images, ceremonies, and palpable examples when needed to reach people whose senses and imagination block comprehension, but remember these are aids to reveal underlying reason and religion, not substitutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciate the different kinds of necessity in reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a logical necessity, a mathematical necessity (hypothetical), and a third real objective necessity apprehended by immediate spiritual consciousness of God as the One and Absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming moral-political judgments, recognize which type of necessity your argument appeals to; claims grounded in spiritual or absolute necessity differ in force from purely logical or hypothetical ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles and ideas are the seed of political power
rubrics_metrics.description: Every principle is actualized by an idea; science (understood as ideas and principles) is power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote coherent, living ideas and principles if you seek durable political influence; mere linked notions or technical calculations influence only the few unless embodied in ideas that reach the many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of explaining heroic action solely by base motives
rubrics_metrics.description: It is inadequate for the mere understanding to account for moral greatness by schemes of motives that reduce heroism to paltry personal interests; nothing great was ever achieved without enthusiasm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and foster the role of genuine enthusiasm and higher motives in public life; avoid reductive historiography that strips nobility from public action and thereby misunderstands causes of great deeds.
